mappings.note: Best conductor of electricity (silver). Physical-property classification, LO-1.
Mercury is the metal in amalgams. Alloy composition, the clause LO-7 owns.
Why metals conduct (free electrons). Conductivity is the physical property LO-1 classifies on; the electron explanation is background, not a separate outcome.
Why metals look dull -- a surface oxide/sulphide film builds up. That is corrosion, LO-7, not the intrinsic lustre of LO-1.
Solid and gaseous non-metals. Physical state, LO-1.
Aluminium foil for food packing -- a use resting on malleability and inertness. Physical-property classification, LO-1.
Whether 2,8,6 loses six or gains two electrons. Valency reasoning from the Bohr configuration, which is the C 1.1 competency; no LO covers it.
Alloys rather than pure metals in heating elements (higher resistivity, no oxidation at red heat). Alloy property, LO-7.
A shining metal blackening on heating in air -> copper, CuO. Metal-plus-oxygen chemical property, LO-1; not LO-7, since this is deliberate heating, not slow atmospheric attack.
Silver blackening with time in air. Corrosion, LO-7.
Another metal carrying a protective oxide film. Self-protection against corrosion, LO-7.
Common feature of metal atoms' configurations (few valence electrons). Atomic structure and the Periodic Table -- C 1.1; LO-1 asks for physical/chemical properties, not configurations.
Definition of ionic compounds. Compound formation by electron transfer, the C 1.1 competency.
A liquid metal and a liquid non-metal. Physical state, LO-1.
Iron nails in CuSO4 for 15 minutes -- observations of a displacement reaction. LO-2.
Amphoteric oxides with an example. Oxide nature, LO-1.
A lustrous non-metal and a non-lustrous metal -- the exceptions to LO-1's physical-property rule.
Electronic configuration of Z = 11. Purely atomic structure, C 1.1; no LO covers writing configurations.
Why metals conduct and non-metals do not. The conductivity contrast used in LO-1 to classify.
Properties that make aluminium industrially valuable (light, malleable, good conductor). Physical properties, LO-1.
Names alloys of aluminium, lead and copper for three uses. Alloying, LO-7.
Why every ore is a mineral but not every mineral an ore. The ore concept that LO-6 is built on.
Two distinct parts: (a) iron knife turning CuSO4 green is a displacement (LO-2) and (b) the green layer on a bronze medal is corrosion of copper (LO-7).

Why titanium is a strategic metal, naming two properties (strength-to-weight, high melting point). Physical-property description, LO-1; its corrosion resistance is a secondary point, not the question.
Copper plate in AgNO3 gives a deposit -- copper displaces silver because it is higher in the series. LO-2. (The stem calls the deposit black, which is wrong; see defect list.)
Zinc displaces mercury but not magnesium. A textbook use of the reactivity series to predict where displacement happens and where it does not -- LO-2.
Mostly ore concentration -- gravity separation versus froth flotation -- which is LO-6; the tail asks for an amalgam example, an alloy, so LO-7 is cited for that part only.
Zinc blende and the roasting that turns it into the oxide. Extraction, LO-6.
Why metals displace hydrogen from acids and non-metals do not. The contrast is metal versus non-metal, so LO-1, rather than the metal-versus-metal ordering of LO-2.
ZnO's amphoteric character and another example. Oxide nature, LO-1. (Stem reads 'atmospheric oxide' for 'amphoteric', and part (b) on alkalis belongs to Acids, Bases and Salts -- see defect list.)
Defines the activity series, orders five metals, and predicts two displacement outcomes. LO-2 throughout; part (c) on a metal hydride is a one-line add-on with no frame slot.
Mercury conducts without electrolysing because conduction there is metallic (LO-1), while pure water does not electrolyse for want of free ions (C 1.1, ionic compounds).
Cinnabar and how mercury is won from it. Extraction of a low-reactivity metal, LO-6.
Part (a) asks the student to devise an experiment showing magnesium above zinc -- C 8.2-LO-2 word for word. Part (b), copper failing to liberate hydrogen, is the reactivity-series content, LO-2.
Judges a claim that air/water behaviour of Na, Mg and Fe reveals their series positions, with examples. LO-2.

Metal carbonate + dilute HCl giving CO2 identified by lime water. No metals-and-non-metals outcome covers carbonate-acid chemistry -- this is Acids, Bases and Salts content sitting in this chapter (see defect list), so the C 1.2 competency on the nature and properties of chemical substances is cited rather than forcing LO-1 or LO-2.
Sorts CO2, SO2 and NO2 from Na2O and CaO by litmus and names them acidic. Oxide nature as the metal/non-metal discriminator, LO-1.
Names the tarnish compounds on silver, copper and iron. Corrosion products, LO-7.

Copper powder blackens on heating and is restored by hydrogen; name the reaction types and write the equations. Metal-oxygen chemistry, LO-1. Not LO-6: no ore and no metallurgy, just a bench redox pair.
(a) Which of Fe, Cu, Mg give hydrogen with dilute HCl -- position relative to hydrogen, LO-2. (b) Why exposed metal surfaces go dull -- corrosion, LO-7.

Asks the student to demonstrate that an ionic solid conducts only once dissolved. The content is ionic structure (C 1.1); the 'how will you demonstrate' framing is inquiry design, cited at C 8.2 because its only LO is restricted to comparing two metals.

Design an activity showing that burning sulphur gives an acidic oxide. Content is the acidic oxide of a non-metal (LO-1); the activity design sits at C 8.2, not C 8.2-LO-2, which is about two metals' reactivity.
Defines corrosion, names rust and the tarnish colours, then lists damage and prevention. Entirely LO-7.
Three independent 'give reasons' parts, one per outcome: zinc displacing copper (LO-2), silver blackening (LO-7), sulphide roasted to oxide before extraction (LO-6).
Roasting/calcination and the copper refining cell are LO-6; the thermite equation for cracked rails is a reactivity-driven displacement, LO-2.
Part (a) picks metals by physical property (LO-1); part (b) is the electrolytic refining of copper with a labelled diagram (LO-6). The kerosene sub-item brushes LO-2 but is one clause of four.
Copper extraction equations and the reducing agent for top-of-series metals are LO-6, covering exactly the low/medium/high split that LO-6 names; the green coating in part (c) is corrosion, LO-7.
Part (a) is LO-6 verbatim -- which reduction method for oxides of less, moderately and highly reactive metals. Part (b) is the thermite displacement, LO-2.

(a) Zinc reacting with NaOH is amphoteric behaviour, a chemical property under LO-1. (b) Metal giving XOH of mass 40 with cold water plus a flammable gas -> sodium, a water-reactivity identification, LO-2.
Full electro-refining of copper: diagram, electrolyte, electrodes, electrode processes. Refining step of LO-6.
Colour of the deposit on a zinc rod in CuSO4 -- observing a displacement. LO-2.
Identity of the reddish-brown coating on an iron nail in CuSO4 (copper). Displacement, LO-2.
Names the reaction type of Fe2O3 + Al -> Al2O3 + Fe (displacement). LO-2.
Picks the correct PROCEDURE for showing zinc is more reactive than copper -- C 8.2-LO-2 exactly (comparing two metals, controlling what varies); LO-2 carries the underlying content.
Names the reddish-brown deposit on iron nails in CuSO4. Same displacement observation as 104527; the frame offers nothing finer, so both take LO-2.
Which rod turns blue CuSO4 pale green (iron). Predicting displacement from relative reactivity, LO-2.

The physical forms zinc and copper come in for lab work (granules, turnings). No content outcome fits; cited at the inquiry competency C 8.2, whose clause on using scientific materials/instruments is the nearest, rather than forcing a chemistry LO.
An iron nail in aluminium sulphate gives no change -- iron is below aluminium. Using the series to predict that displacement does NOT occur, LO-2.
Cu, Fe, Zn and Al strips in ferrous sulphate; which pair reacts. Displacement prediction from the series, LO-2. (Stem is corrupted mid-sentence -- see defect list.)
